summary.whatChanges: In the expect package's equality logic, subset-equality testers are now filtered out before delegating to an asymmetric matcher's `asymmetricMatch`. Recursive subset testers (closures) are tracked in a WeakSet so they can be identified. Tests are added covering asymmetric matchers nested inside `toMatchObject`.
behaviorChanges: Asymmetric matchers (e.g. expect.arrayContaining) used inside toMatchObject now compare their contents with full equality instead of inheriting subset semantics
Assertions like expect([{id:1}]).toMatchObject(expect.arrayContaining([{id:1, required:'x'}])) now fail where they previously passed
Nested cases such as { nested: expect.arrayContaining([{ id: 1 }]) } no longer match array items that carry extra properties
Custom testers passed through to asymmetricMatch no longer include subsetEquality or its recursive closure variants
risks: Existing user test suites relying on the previous lenient subset behavior inside asymmetric matchers will start failing
Identity-based WeakSet tracking only catches subset testers created via subsetEquality; equivalent testers constructed elsewhere or re-wrapped would not be filtered
Filtering removes these testers for all asymmetric matchers, potentially affecting matchers beyond arrayContaining/objectContaining
